chunks: From him, from Ahmad, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from Dorost, who said:

I heard Abu Ibrahim (peace be upon him) saying: When the believer falls ill, God — Mighty and Majestic — reveals unto the companion (Angel) on the left hand side: 'Do not write any sin against My servant for as long as he is in My prison and My fetters'; and He reveals unto the companion (Angel) of the right hand side: 'Write for My servant what you would have written for him during his good health, from the good deeds.'

key_terms.الْحَسَنَاتِ: Good deeds recorded for the sick believer as if performed during health
key_terms.حَبْسِي وَوَثَاقِي: My prison and My fetters — metaphor for illness as a divinely-imposed constraint
key_terms.صَاحِبِ الشِّمَالِ: Companion of the left — the recording angel who writes sins
key_terms.صَاحِبِ الْيَمِينِ: Companion of the right — the recording angel who writes good deeds

ai.seo_question: What does Islam say about the recording of deeds during illness?
ai.summary: Imam Musa al-Kazim (peace be upon him) teaches that when a believer falls sick, God commands the recording angel on the left (who records sins) to cease recording bad deeds, while commanding the angel on the right (who records good deeds) to continue recording good deeds as if the believer were healthy. This hadith uses the imagery of illness as a divine 'prison' and 'fetter' — a suffering imposed by God — which consequently exempts the believer from recording of sins. It belongs to the classical Shia theological understanding that trials and illness, being God's decree, bear spiritual benefit for the faithful.
